title: My kids are petrified going to Shepherd's Bush, says Laila Cunningham after stabbing
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Laila Cunningham tells how she has brought up her children](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/9ec17174-20a8-5108-b76c-a892fc39daa3/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![Bus driver Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa died after being shot on Monday evening in Clapham (Metropolitan Police/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/12/18/10d77b27d5b3de0bfdc57923c38f4a4cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg2NjQxNDg4-2.85545879.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“My own kids swim in Shepherd’s Bush. They’re now petrified of going there. And as their mum so am I.
“We were there last weekend. It increasingly feels like nowhere is safe.
“Sadiq Khan can keep telling us London is safe, but that means very little to families living with this fear,” she added.
But Sir Sadiq has rejected claims of a “lawless London” with high numbers of shootings and stabbings.
Earlier this week, he hit out at Donald Trump and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK who have sought to argue that the capital is plagued by crime.
He posted on X: “The loudest voices online aren't always the most accurate.
“New data shows our homicide rate is lower than every US state, while murder rates are at record lows.
“The evidence is clear: our approach to tackling crime and its causes works. It’s driving down violence right across the capital.”
![Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said the research ‘proves we were right to act’ (Victoria Jones/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/07/6cf18c2a55353082ea87aedde5a23035Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTQ0ODM2-2.75224103.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Scotland Yard said a man, aged 48, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after a woman was fatally stabbed in Shepherd’s Bush, west London.
Read More
Police were called to reports of a stabbing shortly before 8.30am on Tuesday, 18 August, at an address on Askew Road, Shepherd’s Bush.
Officers attended the scene with the London Ambulance Service where two women, aged 52 and 32, were found with stab wounds.
Despite the best efforts of medical professionals, the older woman was pronounced dead at the scene.
Her next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by specially-trained officers.
The 32-year-old woman was taken to hospital.
Detective Inspector Richard MacKenzie, who is leading the investigation, said: “We believe this to be an isolated incident within a residential address, but we know it will cause concern locally.”
There were 97 homicides in the capital in 2025, down 36 per cent from 153 in 2019 and 11 per cent fewer than the 109 in 2024.
The Met said last year also had the lowest killings since 95 took place 11 years ago in 2014.
The force stated that 2025 saw a homicide rate of 1.1 per 100,000 people - safer than comparable global cities such as New York at 2.8, Paris (1.6), Toronto (1.6), Berlin (3.2), Los Angeles (5.6), Chicago (11.7), and Philadelphia (12.3).
Just days ago, detectives investigating the murder of 25-year-old Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa renewed their appeal for information.
The Transport for London bus driver died on Willington Road, Clapham, at around 10pm on Monday, 10 August.
Following the shooting, officers arrested a 22-year-old man on suspicion of murder after he attended hospital with a gunshot wound.
He was later discharged and released with no further action following further police enquiries.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/16/01M0AJ3H1BBYM2JA29BGJV0VQD.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Separately, detectives launched a murder investigation after a man in his 40s was found inside a vehicle with gunshot wounds at around 3am on Tuesday August 18.
summary: Following a fatal stabbing in Shepherd's Bush, local concerns about safety have grown, with residents expressing fear despite London Mayor Sadiq Khan defending the capital's safety record and citing declining homicide rates. Police arrested a 48-year-old man on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after two women were stabbed at a residential address on Askew Road. Meanwhile, detectives are also investigating separate fatal incidents involving firearms, including the shooting of a bus driver in Clapham.
key_points: A 52-year-old woman was killed and a 32-year-old woman was injured in a stabbing on Askew Road in Shepherd's Bush.
A 48-year-old man was arrested by Scotland Yard on suspicion of murder and attempted murder regarding the Shepherd's Bush incident.
Mayor Sadiq Khan rejected claims of a lawless London, stating that data shows record low murder rates and a lower homicide rate than every US state.
Police are conducting separate investigations into other fatal incidents, including the shooting of bus driver Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa in Clapham.

key_points: Average house prices in central London slumped by 25.4%, wiping nearly £300,000 off the average price.
First-time buyers in the borough paid an average of £766,000 in June, down 25.3% from the previous year.
Other boroughs also recorded declines, including Tower Hamlets down 13.1%, Islington down 8.1%, and Camden down 7.1%.
Experts attribute prime central London's long-term price falls to higher stamp duty, the ending of non-dom status, and diminished appeal for landlords.

title: London’s first official bathing area hit by toxic algae outbreak
author: Maryam Zakir-Hussain
content:
London’s first official bathing spot has been hit by a toxic algal bloom, as swimmers have been warned to avoid the river.
The Ham and Kingston site on the Thames became a bathing spot as recently as May this year.
However, the Environment Agency (EA) issued a formal notice on Tuesday cautioning against swimming, warning: “Bathing is not advised, due to pollution from harmful algae.”
Staff from the regulator have taken samples of the water since May, checking for harmful bacteria and to establish the water quality.
Marlene Lawrence, who founded local swimming group Teddington Bluetits said swam in the river before the warning notice was issued.
![London ’s Ham and Kingston on the Thames has been hit by a toxic algal bloom](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/13/07/PA-85591021-3b704fb8.jpeg)
“Instantly on Sunday night I came out in a really bad rash, itchy spots, and that’s not like me. I can only attribute it to the algae in the river,” she told The Times.
The semi-retired swimmer, who helped secure the site as a bathing spot, first noticed signs of algae last week.
She believes the consecutive record-breaking heatwaves are behind the water pollution.
According to the EA, during an algal bloom, the water becomes less clear and may become blue-green or greenish-brown.
Scums can form during calm weather when several bloom-forming species rise to the surface. This can look like paint, mousse or small clumps.
Cyanobacteria or ‘blue-green algae’, a type of blooming algae, can produce toxins. These toxins can kill wild animals, livestock and pets. They can also harm people, producing rashes after skin contact and illnesses if swallowed.
An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “We have identified blue-green algae on the lower River Thames including the Ham and Kingston designated bathing water.
“We are working with the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames, who have put signage in this location to warn people that it is not safe to swim.
“An advice against bathing notice has been activated on the Swiminfo website.”
The spokesperson also warned that it was likely the section of the River Thames between Hampton and Kingston had also been affected.
“It is important that members of public do not enter the Thames along this stretch. It is also vitally important to keep dogs out of the water,” they urged.
![Cyanobacteria or ‘blue-green algae’, a type of blooming algae, can produce toxins](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/13/18/PA-76925632-92d43734.jpeg)
It comes as a sobering new assessment has revealed that a mere 14 per cent of England’s rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.
The findings come from the Environment Agency’s first update in six years, conducted under retained EU legislation governing water quality.
This comprehensive evaluation scrutinised 4,658 of the country’s rivers, lakes, estuaries, canals, and coastal waters, measuring their health against a range of standards including wildlife populations, overall water quality, and the condition of physical habitats.
The report indicates that just 14.3 per cent of surface water bodies achieved an overall good ecological status in 2025, with widespread issues attributed to sewage spills, agricultural nutrient runoff, and pollutants emanating from urban areas and roads, such as litter, petrol, and garden pesticides.
summary: London's first official bathing spot at Ham and Kingston on the Thames has been hit by a toxic blue-green algal bloom, prompting warnings from the Environment Agency advising the public not to swim. Swimmers have reported rashes following contact with the water, and authorities have urged people and dogs to stay out of the affected stretch between Hampton and Kingston. The incident coincides with a broader Environment Agency assessment revealing that only 14.3 per cent of England's surface waters achieved good ecological status in 2025.
key_points: The Environment Agency issued a formal warning advising against swimming at London's first official bathing site in Ham and Kingston due to toxic blue-green algae.
Local swimmers have reported developing rashes and itchy spots after entering the water before the warning was issued.
Authorities have erected warning signs and advised the public to keep both themselves and their dogs out of the affected stretch of the Thames.
A recent Environment Agency assessment reported that only 14.3 per cent of England's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.

title: London's Night Tube celebrates 10 years
author: Kesewaa Browne; Amy Clarke
content:
![Entrance to a London Underground station at night, illuminated by streetlights and a blue sign reading âNight Tube - Launching tonight.â People walk near the station entrance, with city buildings, traffic, and a red double-decker bus visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/698c/live/94e4a730-9ae4-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Signs announcing the Night Tube shine above Oxford Circus station
- Published
Ten years and 67 million passengers later, London's Night Tube is a vital part of the capital's infrastructure. But what was it like to work its opening night?
The evening of 19 August 2016: Lovely Obeng, a 19-year-old customer service assistant, started her first night shift at Tottenham Court Road station.
"The very first night of Night Tube was very exciting, I must admit," she said.
"There was so much going on; everyone had been looking forward to that particular night - the customers were very excited."
The first night proved there was a demand for the service - more than 50,000 journeys were made between 00:30 and 05:30 on the Victoria and Central lines, the two lines first to launch.
Now, the service - which runs on Fridays and Saturdays - has expanded to include the Jubilee, Northern, Piccadilly and Windrush lines and records an average of more than 81,000 journeys each night.
![A station staff member in a blue uniform stands near the ticket gates in a bright, modern station. A radio and body-worn camera are attached to the uniform, with a control room visible behind glass windows and accessible ticket barriers in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/04b5/live/01d24150-9ae9-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Lovely Obeng, 29, has worked for Transport for London since she was 19 years old
Looking back, Obeng said staff felt they were witnessing a significant moment for London's transport network.
"Working the launch night, as a team, we all felt like we were part of something great," she said.
"It was something that was new and we could feel that and it was something that TfL (Transport for London) as a company worked very hard towards making that happen.
"So I must admit that I did feel like a part of history."
Working in central London meant she saw first-hand the reaction from passengers - there was a "buzz around the whole city".
"I think London needed it because it was an encouragement for our night life here," she added.
'Sense of joy'
Obeng explained that during that first night, people were particularly excited to utilise the Night Tube for getting home after a night out.
"We also had working customers that were commuting from night shifts themselves or going into early morning shifts," she said, adding that customers kept thanking the team and were grateful for the service during that first weekend.
"There was a sense of joy amongst the city here at Tottenham Court Road," she said.
![Passengers and Sadiq Khan sit together and chat inside the carriage, with Tube safety notices and advertisements visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2a00/live/9f3270a0-9ae4-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan travelled with passengers on a northbound Victoria line Tube train during launch night
Plans for the Night Tube were announced in November 2013, with TfL citing growing demand for overnight travel.
But the service did not arrive without controversy.
Night Tube trains had originally been slated to start in September 2015, but the launch was delayed following a bitter dispute between TfL and rail unions over pay and working conditions.
After months of negotiations and industrial action, the service was given the green light.
Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, joined passengers on the Night Tube during the launch just months after he was appointed as the capital's mayor in May.
At the time, TfL claimed the service could add Â£360m to the economy over 30 years, and it was hoped it would help reinvigorate the night-time economy.
Looking back, he said: "Travelling on the first-ever Night Tube is one of my favourite memories as mayor.
"Through a decade of late nights and early starts, airport journeys and epic trips, morning shifts and nights out that go on for as long as you like, the Night Tube has become a defining feature of London as a world-leading 24/7 city."
Since launch, the service has operated each week apart from during the Covid pandemic when services were suspended in March 2020 and returned in stages from late 2021. The full network was restored by July 2022.
![A London Underground service information board covered with handwritten song suggestions for a âNight Tube Playlist.â The board includes titles such as âNight Fever,â âOne More Night,â âLove Train,â and âDark Side of the Moon,â along with doodles and notes from passengers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/808/cpsprodpb/7f5d/live/2b5fd660-9ae7-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.png)
Passengers were asked to add to the Night Tube playlist on launch night
For Obeng, some of her strongest memories are not of major events or busy weekends, but of individual passengers.
One particular encounter has stayed with her throughout her career.
"My first few months in we had a young lady that was around the same age as me travelling through from a night out and she had literally lost all her friends, she'd lost all her belongings," she said.
"I remember her coming into the station and looking at me and she just burst out in tears."
Obeng said she discovered the pair had a lot in common and took the passenger into the control room where staff managed to reach out to an emergency contact.
"We managed to get her home safely on Night Tube. That memory will stand with me for my entire career with TfL."
![London Underground train wrapped in a galaxy-themed design at a station platform, with passengers visible through the windows. Large white text on the train reads âThe Night Tube,â alongside Transport for London and Mayor of London branding.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/de8d/live/8ea62470-9ae4-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
The carriages were decorated to celebrate the launch in 2016
Every shift is different
Experiences like that, she said, showed that the job involved much more than helping people catch trains.
"One day I might have to become a first aider, one day I become a therapist, one day I become somebody's friend," she said.
"Every day is different because especially while you're working on Night Tube, you don't know what is going to come your way. You have to be prepared for all scenarios and all situations."
Obeng described the night shifts as "not easy" but they had "taught her so much" and made her "resilient".
Now 29, Obeng moved to day shifts for the first time since the overnight service began.
"I did want to experience a different style of the station and the different passenger flow" but "night shift will be a part of me forever."
What's next for Night Tube?
Despite Thursday's growing reputation as London's "new Friday", with many office workers increasingly treating it as the start of the weekend and fuelling the capital's night-time economy, TfL said there were no plans to introduce the services on Thursday nights or expand the service to other Underground lines.
The transport body said any expansion would require additional funding and significant changes to overnight maintenance schedules but "could be considered once major TfL modernisation programmes are complete".

summary: London's Night Tube has marked its tenth anniversary after serving 67 million passengers since launching on August 19, 2016. Initially delayed by disputes over pay and conditions, the overnight service has since expanded to six lines and now records over 81,000 journeys each night. Transport for London currently has no plans to add Thursday services or expand to further lines due to funding and maintenance schedules.
key_points: London's Night Tube launched on August 19, 2016, initially running on the Victoria and Central lines.
The launch was delayed from September 2015 due to a dispute between TfL and rail unions over pay and working conditions.
Over ten years and 67 million passengers later, the service has expanded to include the Jubilee, Northern, Piccadilly, and Windrush lines.
TfL currently has no plans to introduce Thursday night services or expand further without additional funding and changes to maintenance schedules.

title: Peckham’s legendary car boot is launching a new market in east London
author: Eloise Feilden
content:
[title]
Thrifters, bargain hunters and fashionistas – we have excellent news. One of south London’s finest car boot sales is expanding east.
If you’ve never experienced the wonders of Peckham Car Boot, well, what have you been doing with your Sunday mornings? For the past seven years, new and veteran resellers have flogged everything from pre-loved pieces by big-name brands to vintage homewares out the trunks of their cars at the bi-monthly market.
Erin Murphy and Steven Lopes, the duo behind the swap meet, launched an additional iteration last year to serve second-hand treasure hunters in Balham. Now, they’ve announced that they will also be bringing the weekend market north of the river. From September, Peckham Car Boot is heading to Leyton, hosting monthly events at George Mitchell School in September, October and November.
The organisers have said that they’ll be using these three events as a trial run, and will look to make the event permanent if it’s popular with the E10 crowd.
Londoners with an N postcode shouldn’t feel left out, though, because Peckham Car Boot is also planning to trial a market in Stokey. Yep, it’ll be heading to Stoke Newington School for three monthly events from September to ‘test the waters’. Its founders are encouraging sellers and shoppers to ‘come down, see what it's about, and help us decide if this is a regular thing’.
![Peckham Car Boot](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438133/image.webp) 
If you’re looking to offload some old gear, bookings are already open for both the east and north London markets, with pitch prices starting at £15. If there was ever a time to have a good ol’ attic clean-out, this might just be it.
All the dates of Peckham Car Boot’s east and north London markets
Leyton Car Boot
- September 6
- October 4
- November 1
Stoke Newington Car Boot
- September 20
- October 18
- November 15

summary: The organisers of the popular Peckham Car Boot sale are expanding to east and north London with upcoming trial markets in Leyton and Stoke Newington. Running from September through November, these monthly events will help founders determine if there is enough demand to make them permanent. Pitch bookings for sellers are currently open with prices starting at £15.
key_points: Peckham Car Boot is launching trial markets in Leyton and Stoke Newington starting in September.
The new markets will be held monthly for three months to test popularity before potentially becoming permanent.
Leyton events will take place at George Mitchell School, while Stoke Newington events will be held at Stoke Newington School.
Pitch bookings for the new east and north London locations are currently open with prices starting at £15.

title: Must-see London art exhibitions closing in August 2026
author: Anny Shaw
content:
Must-see London art exhibitions closing in August 2026
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Dame Tracey Emin exhibition to launch at Tate Modern](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/834a99c1-70e6-4159-89ad-86a66723986e/thumbnail-360.webp)
August is when the art world’s movers and shakers decamp to yachts and the Balearics, leaving London’s museums and galleries in a summer lull. The big autumn openings are still a few weeks away, but before everyone swaps the Med for Frieze week there are plenty of reasons to stay in town. Several of the year’s hottest exhibitions are entering their final days, from blockbuster surveys to quieter discoveries. Here are the ones worth catching before they vanish.
David Hockney: A Year in Normandie
Serpentine North Gallery until August 23
![Thomas Mupfupi Resting on a Pink and White Checkered Tablecloth](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/15/07/David-Hockney-art.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
David Hockney’s iPad pictures cannot be compared to the brilliance of his early paintings of turquoise swimming pools in Los Angeles, but there is something beguiling about the 90-metre-long frieze at the centre of this exhibition. Stitched together from 100 iPad paintings printed on to a single ribbon of paper, the epic work captures the changing seasons in Normandy and was inspired by the Bayeux Tapestry, which coincidentally goes on show at the British Museum on September 10. Hockney, who collaborated with the Serpentine on this presentation, died in June at 88. Due to a surge in public interest, opening times have been extended until 9pm on August 21 and 22.
Barbara Hepworth in Colour
Courtauld until September 6
Barbara Hepworth is usually associated with the cool, pale stone and polished wood of her abstract sculptures, but this illuminating show reveals an artist who had a far more nuanced relationship with colour. Deep blues, vivid reds, greens and yellows punctuate her carved forms and drawings where colour is deftly used to create the illusion of depth. Her move to St Ives in 1939 transformed these experiments: pale blue came to evoke the Cornish sky and sea, while taut red strings suggested the tension of wind, water and hills. Yet the roots of this palette predated Cornwall, in Hepworth’s encounters with Mondrian and European modernism.
A revealing rethink of a familiar artist.
Hurvin Anderson
Tate Britain until August 23
At first glance, Hurvin Anderson’s paintings look like celebrations of colour: lush greens, electric blues, purples and pinks conjure the tropical landscapes of Jamaica and Trinidad. But his retrospective also reveals something more complicated. Born in Birmingham to Jamaican parents, Anderson has spent three decades painting between Britain and the Caribbean. His pictures of the latter are repeatedly interrupted by fences, grilles and chicken wire, geometric devices that become visual and conceptual barriers. Darker, hazier paintings recall the Handsworth of his childhood — football in Handsworth Park, swimming pools and the makeshift barbershops that became social hubs for Caribbean immigrants. The result is a compelling examination of what it means to belong.
Summer Exhibition 2026
Royal Academy until August 23
![Gallery view of the Summer Exhibition at Royal Academy of Arts](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/15/32/Gallery-view-of-the-Summer-Exhibition-at-Royal-Academy-of-Arts-2026.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Much like shopping in your local charity shop, you must be prepared to rummage through the dross to find the gems in the RA Summer Exhibition of 1,851 works. Several comedians are trying their hand at art: Joe Lycett pictures Cilla Black in a rather unflattering light, while Harry Hill has two bizarre paintings of burning cars. Even more bizarre (but strangely pleasing) is a video of a man doing David Bowie karaoke. At the more established end of the spectrum, there are hits and misses, too. Try to ignore Ugo Rondinone’s LED rainbow sculpture spelling “the song is you” in the courtyard and head straight for Frank Bowling’s multi-coloured offering instead. Interconnectedness is the theme, according to artist Ryan Gander, who has co-ordinated this year’s show, though that feels more like a challenge than manifesto.
Zurbarán
National Gallery until August 23
Francisco de Zurbarán’s first major UK exhibition brings together more than 40 works, from monumental altarpieces to exquisitely observed still lifes. Most powerful are the intense, mystical works of the Baroque Spanish master’s early Seville years. Take, for example, The Crucifixion (1627), in which Christ’s pale, muscular body emerges from near-total darkness, an image so illusional early viewers thought it a sculpture. The Apparition of Saint Peter to Saint Peter Nolasco (1629), which portrays a dream-like scene of a crucified man falling through space, is stranger still. A remarkably modern take on deep, if unnerving, spirituality.
Tracey Emin: A Second Life
Tate Modern until August 31
![An artwork from Tracey Emin's Tate Modern EXHIBITION 2026](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/15/01/Tracey-Emin-Tate-Modern-EXHIBITION-2026.jpeg?trim=985,1095,1141,1006&quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Few artists can do it like Emin, who has attained icon status. Early appliqué blankets, spidery prints and show-stoppingly candid videos about why she never became a mother are hung alongside archival material: family photographs and handwritten poetry, offering a no-holds-barred window on to the artist’s suffering, pain and joy. My Bed (1998) also makes an appearance, writ large in contemporary art history but surprisingly delicate in real life.
Cecily Brown: Picture Making
Serpentine South Gallery until September 6
Cecily Brown’s first major UK institutional show in more than 20 years is a homecoming of sorts. Based in New York since 1994, the London-born painter turns to memories of the English countryside and nearby Kensington Gardens for a new series of landscapes, where trees, water, animals and figures emerge and dissolve among her gestural brushstrokes. But nature here is never entirely benign. Woodland idylls tip into something darker and more unstable; beauty seems perpetually on the verge of unravelling. Brown’s landscapes may be fantastical, but their sense of a natural world in flux feels unnervingly familiar viewed during a summer of extreme heat and wildfires.
Project a Black Planet
Barbican until September 6
Pan-Africanism is the sprawling subject of this ambitious exhibition, which brings together more than 250 works from Africa, the Caribbean, Brazil, North America and Europe, spanning a century. Paintings by El Anatsui, Claudette Johnson and Lynette Yiadom-Boakye sit alongside photography, film, posters, journals and archival material, tracing ideas of black identity, resistance, liberation and solidarity. It is a demanding show — its curatorial arguments can sometimes threaten to overwhelm the art — but there are moments of real power, particularly in Johnson’s charged self-portraits. Allow plenty of time: this is an exhibition to explore rather than skim.
summary: London galleries and museums feature several notable art exhibitions closing in August and September 2026. The featured shows cover a wide variety of works, including David Hockney's Normandy frieze at the Serpentine North Gallery, Barbara Hepworth's color experiments at the Courtauld, and Francisco de Zurbarán's Baroque masterpieces at the National Gallery. Other highlighted exhibitions include displays by Hurvin Anderson, Tracey Emin, Cecily Brown, and the Royal Academy's Summer Exhibition.
key_points: David Hockney's exhibition at the Serpentine North Gallery features a 90-metre-long iPad painting frieze capturing Normandy's changing seasons.
The Courtauld's Barbara Hepworth exhibition explores the artist's use of deep blues, reds, greens, and yellows in her carved forms and drawings.
Tate Britain's Hurvin Anderson retrospective examines his paintings of tropical Caribbean landscapes alongside barriers like fences and grilles.
Francisco de Zurbarán's major UK exhibition at the National Gallery brings together over 40 works, including mystical early Seville pieces.
Tracey Emin's exhibition at Tate Modern includes appliqué blankets, personal videos, archival material, and her famous work My Bed.

title: Hundreds of artists to be turfed out of ‘lifeline’ studios by London council
author: Josef Steen; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: Is the capital pushing creatives out?](https://cdn.ex.co/video-uploads/production/0010J00001k7YR6QAM/6e005100-6200-4500-8800-500061006e00-thumbnail.jpeg?cb=1784538548137)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Roughly 230 artists and creatives occupying “lifeline” studios based in high-rises on the Regent’s Park Estate must leave their studio spaces by January 2027, after the council raised risks stemming from changes to building safety legislation.
In 2022, the council moved residents living at Cartmel, Langdale and Coniston housing blocks due to the disruption of HS2 construction nearby, which will eventually see the buildings redeveloped. Together with Bow Arts Trust, the council then transformed the “virtually uninhabitable” flats inside into affordable studios for the local artist community for temporary use.
However, the mixed-use blocks now fall into a fire safety “grey area” due to their height, meaning they are unlikely to meet inspection standards. The council says any temporary improvements would not be financially viable because the buildings are slated for eventual demolition.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/7/05/andy_studio20260812_130537.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The occupants are now scrambling to find new studios, prompting supporters to petition the council to rehouse them. Speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS), children’s book author Andy Stanton said the studios had been “life-changing”, and lamented the dearth of affordable studio spaces in North London, “especially in Camden”.
Mr Stanton is best known for the “Mr Gum” series, for which he won the first Roald Dahl Funny Prize.
He moved into Langdale in March last year, where he found “a whole community of people, at many different stages of life, all needing a place to get something out of themselves for whatever reason”.
‘People are devastated’
He added: “We all knew it was going to be temporary, but suddenly the accelerator has been put down. It’s a real shame, and we’re imploring the council to look at making spaces available.”
Painter Jennifer Louise Martin said her studio in Cartmel was the first affordable space she’d found in the borough. “I’ve had studios across London for the last ten years, and they’re usually offices that are disused or about to be knocked down, but hardly any have been near where I live. Because I’ve got young kids, I was really chuffed to find somewhere in Camden,” she said.
Numerous arts charities and organisations have highlighted the financial struggles affecting artists across the capital in recent years. A 2022 King’s College London study stated that 13,780 creatives were on a waiting list for spaces deemed affordable. Since that year, studio rents have risen faster than inflation, and in 2025, a survey by London’s Affordable Artists Studio Network (LAASN) found studio rents had risen above £20 per sq ft of space for the first time.
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan has warned that artists were being “priced out of neighbourhoods they helped to regenerate”. In January, City Hall committed £2.2m to reverse the decline in studios, claiming this would support artists to put down roots locally.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/7/39/Jennifer_Louise_Martin.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Ms Martin added: “A lot of people are devastated. We were told it was going to be a rolling contract, but I never thought it would be this soon. If I had, I probably wouldn’t have invested so much money into the studio.”
Read More
The painter also argued that the council could also lose out as a result of the local artists leaving the building, since the local authority regularly commissioned work from them for its cultural programme. “Have they thought about where they will recruit us from if we lose our spaces to work in the borough?” she said.
Marcel Baettig, CEO of Bow Arts Trust, told the LDRS the charity was “devastated” the studio initiative was coming to a “premature” end, and would seek to work with Camden Council to find alternative spaces.
“These spaces are vitally important—a lifeline for emerging creative people who contribute so much to the cultural life of Camden and Greater London,” he said. “The loss of an affordable studio is about much more than losing a place to work. For many artists, it can mean the end of their career and the loss of their ability to remain part of London’s creative community.”
Cllr James Slater, Cabinet Member for Planning and a Sustainable Camden, said the “innovative” use of the blocks as studios was “always temporary”.
“We recognise that this is disappointing for the studio occupiers affected and we are in the early stages of investigating possible accommodation elsewhere in the borough,” he told the LDRS.
summary: Approximately 230 artists and creatives must vacate their temporary studio spaces on the Regent's Park Estate by January 2027 due to building safety legislation concerns. The council stated that making the mixed-use blocks compliant is financially unviable because the buildings are slated for eventual demolition following HS2 disruption. Occupants and arts organizations have expressed devastation over the closure, highlighting a severe lack of affordable studio spaces in London.
key_points: About 230 artists must leave their studios at Cartmel, Langdale, and Coniston housing blocks by January 2027.
The council cited building safety legislation and height issues as the reason for the eviction, noting that temporary repairs are financially unviable due to planned demolition.
The spaces were originally transformed into affordable studios for temporary use after residents were moved out due to HS2 construction disruption.
Affected artists and the Bow Arts Trust are calling on the council to help find alternative local accommodation.
London faces a broader crisis of rising studio rents and a high demand for affordable creative workspaces.

title: Zendaya And Tom Holland Just Revealed Their Favourite London Restaurants
author: Amelia Morgan
content:
![](https://www.thehandbook.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1920,height=1120,fit=cover,q=80,format=webp/https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/zendaya-1.jpg)
Hollywood’s favourite couple has officially spoken. According to appetiteapp.uk, these are Zendaya and Tom Holland‘s go-to London restaurants, and the list doesn’t hold back. From must-try Indian spots to cult-favourite pubs, here’s where the couple actually eats.
Jamavar
Jamavar in Mayfair is the Michelin-starred jewel of London’s Indian dining scene, with dishes drawing on royal Mughal cooking as well as coastal South Indian flavours. Think slow-cooked biryanis and tandoor classics alongside coconut and curry-leaf specialities from Kerala. Led by chef Surender Mohan, it’s the kind of grand, palace-inspired spot that suits a date night as much as a celebration.
Where: 8 Mount St, London W1K 3NF
Website: www.jamavar.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/jamavar-onam-4-1-scaled.jpg)
The Devonshire
The Devonshire on Denman Street is Soho’s ultimate two-in-one: a proper, no-frills pub downstairs with a legendary pint of Guinness, and a wood ember grill restaurant upstairs serving dry-aged Scottish beef, langoustines and hand-dived scallops. It’s the rare spot that works equally well for a casual pint or a full-blown special-occasion dinner.
Where: The Devonshire, 17 Denman St, London W1D 7HW
Website: www.thedevonshire.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/the-devonshire-pub-dining-room.jpg)
Ottolenghi, Chelsea
Tucked away on Chelsea’s Pavilion Road, Ottolenghi Chelsea is the deli-restaurant hybrid the brand is famous for. It’s an all-day spot, so it’s just as good for a coffee and almond croissant on the terrace as it is for a full lunch of Ottolenghi’s signature vibrant, veg-forward cooking.
Where: 261 Pavilion Rd, London SW1X 0BP
Website: www.ottolenghi.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/pvl-lunch.webp)
Scott’s Richmond
Scott’s Richmond brings the glamour of the Mayfair original to the riverside, with Head Chef Tom Fraser serving up seafood classics alongside dishes inspired by its Thames-side setting. For the full experience, head Upstairs at Scott’s for cocktails, Champagne and panoramic river views. It’s polished, seafood-forward glamour with a decidedly scenic backdrop.
Where: 4 Whittaker Ave, Richmond TW9 1EH
Website: www.scottsrichmond.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/contact-us-johnny-stephens-photography-16-0e8a7902-edit.jpg)
The River Cafe
The River Cafe in Hammersmith is a bona fide London institution, set right on the Thames at Thames Wharf. Famous for its authentic, ingredient-led Italian cooking (and a stack of bestselling cookbooks to match), it’s the kind of legendary spot that pairs a serious wine list with an easy, riverside setting.
Where: Thames Wharf, Rainville Rd, London W6 9HA
Website: www.rivercafe.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/611134394ddc0e6b4567aa20-trc-restaurant.jpeg)
J Sheekey
Tucked into St Martin’s Court in the heart of theatreland, J Sheekey has been serving up London’s best seafood since 1896. With its famous ruby-red frontage, central crustacean bar and walls lined with photos of famous faces past, it’s earned its reputation as the ultimate post-theatre haunt. 130 years in, still one of the most iconic tables in town.
Where: 28-32 St Martin’s Ct, London WC2N 4AL
Website: www.jsheekey.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/ch-dryjan24-0522-edit-scaled-e1758023511190-1.jpg)
Pahli Hill Bandra Bhai
In Fitzrovia, Pahli Hill Bandra Bhai brings the bylanes and beach shacks of Mumbai to London across two very different rooms: a bright, table-focused space upstairs, and a moodier, low-lit cocktail den below. Voted London’s Best Indian Restaurant by FACT in 2025 and holding a Michelin Bib Gourmand, it’s regional Indian cooking with genuine buzz behind it.
Where: 79-81 Mortimer St, London W1W 7SJ
Website: www.pahlihillbandrabhai.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/join-us-for-christmas.jpg)
The Cocoanut
Down in Kingston upon Thames, The Cocoanut is a proper neighbourhood find – a third-generation, family-run Thai kitchen that’s been serving up authentic dishes since 2010. Expect all the classics done well, from Thai fish cakes to a fiery beef salad, in a relaxed, dog-friendly setting that’s a world away from the West End’s polish.
Where: 16 Mill St, Kingston upon Thames KT1 2RF
Website: www.thecocoanut.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/rwrm3mgvcww8llz7sghw-1.webp)
summary: Zendaya and Tom Holland's favorite London restaurants have been revealed, highlighting a diverse mix of dining spots across the city. The curated list features everything from Michelin-starred Indian cuisine and historic seafood establishments to relaxed neighborhood cafes and popular pubs. These establishments span multiple areas of London, offering distinct culinary experiences from royal Mughal cooking to authentic Thai dishes.
key_points: Jamavar in Mayfair offers Michelin-starred Indian dining with royal Mughal and coastal South Indian flavors.
The Devonshire in Soho combines a ground-floor pub serving Guinness with an upstairs wood ember grill.
J Sheekey in theatreland has been serving seafood since 1896 and is known as a post-theatre haunt.
The Cocoanut in Kingston upon Thames is a third-generation, family-run Thai kitchen operating since 2010.

title: 17 simply smashing things to do in London next month – from food festivals to live music, stunning exhibitions, floating museums, and more
author: Sam Barker
content:
![the famous st pauls cathedral of london during sunset](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/18173758/shutterstock_2458359623-1024x683.jpg) 
As August and the summer weather slowly come to a close, we’re turning our eyes to September, and all that’s in store for us in London. But fret not – the summer isn’t quite over yet. After all, it’s not officially autumn until late September!
You don’t quite need to head inside to make buckets of hot chocolate just yet. And while we can probably expect the temperatures to drop, there are still a few summer-y days in store. Regardless of the weather, with everything going on, there’ll be no pleas to ‘wake me up when September ends’. Here’s our rundown of simply smashing things to do in London this September.
![a crowd of festival attendees at the Siren Stage at Waterworks 2023](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/09183210/230916_WATERWORKS_2023_RobJones_%40hirobjones_%40khromacollectiveIMG_5531-1024x683.jpeg)
While festival season pretty much draws to a close in August, there are still a few events to enjoy in the city if you love live music. Check out the following festivals to wring the most out of 2026’s summer of fests:
🎶 Waterworks Extended (September 12-13): the cancelled festival will instead take the form of a massive 36-hour-long party at The Cause.
🎵 HowTheLightGetsIn London 2026 (September 19-20): the world’s largest philosophy & music festival.
![people milling about in front of a stage emblazoned with a sign for celebrasia](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/22163650/celebrASIA-at-Battersea-Power-Station-c-Brendan-Bell-2-1024x683.jpg)
Cekebrasia returns this September with an enormous celebration of South East Asia. The FREE-to-visit culture and food festival features a huge range of vendors, attractions, live performances, and activations that celebrate the incredible diversity of food, culture, and creativity across the 11 ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) member countries.
Visitors can expect to find over 35 food and drink vendors, an artisan market with more than 50 traders, live music, craft workshops, cooking classes, and more.
![two people playing in a huge ball pit with dark pink walls at Bubble Planet](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/19172251/Bubble-Planet-16-1024x683.jpg)
Bubble Planet is a wild and wonderful immersive experience that surrounds visitors with a seemingly never-ending world (planet?) of bubbles. As you make your way through themed rooms, you’ll explore fantastical landscapes and even step aboard a hot air balloon flight simulator. It’s a feast for the senses, and a true joy to experience
Celebrate Black culture and creativity
![people milling about trafalgar square on a sunny day at the 'Black on the Square' celebration](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/05130233/BlackOnTheSq_0147MRES-1024x683.jpg)
Black on the Square is a FREE annual event in London’s Trafalgar Square that celebrates and highlights Black culture and creativity. It’s a chance to acknowledge and celebrate “the people and communities who contribute to the capital’s creativity”. All are welcome to enjoy the food, entertainment, workshops, activities, stalls, and more.
Find out more here.
Feast on meat at Meatopia
![a food vendor at meatopia, stood at a stand with a large boat behind them, carving meat to portion into servings for festival attendees](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/18102252/September-01-2024-untitled-shootEV1A3198-1024x683.jpg)
Meatopia is a love letter to BBQ, where hungry Londoners can feast on meat to their heart’s content. Going strong since 2013, when it crossed the pond from New York, where the festival was founded, Meatopia offers up 4 days of delicious food from “some of the very best live-fire chefs from UK, Europe and the World”.
Find out more and grab your tickets here.
![London Eye as seen from up high with the House of Parliament and River Thames behind it](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/23095652/London-Eye-Rebrand-Drone-Photography-39-1024x767.jpg)
Think the London Eye is only for tourists? Think again! Many people, even local Londoners, probably don’t know that you can spot some real gems from up there – things you had no idea you could see from the heart of London.
This summer, book yourself a ticket for a ride in one of the capsules and look out for these lesser-known sights, including the centuries-old Cleopatra’s Needle, two hidden rooftop gardens, a couple of castles, and much more.
![The exterior of Senate House (left), the St Pancras clocktower (right)](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/15092417/Copy-of-FACEBOOK-SPLIT-IMAGE-34-1024x576.jpg)
The London Open House Festival returns to London this September, giving us mere mortals the chance to cross the threshold of some of the city’s most exclusive establishments. Hundreds of sites across the city will be throwing open their (usually firmly locked) doors for the occasion, including the likes of:
🏦 OXO Tower
👀 Old Royal Naval College
🏦 English National Ballet
👀 Senate House
🏦 St Pancras Chambers and Clock Tower
👀 BBC Broadcasting House
and many more!
![Sabrage acctress dressed in fancy dress with gloves surrounded by bottles of bubbly](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/30094930/She-doesnt-just-walk-the-walk-she-walks-on-bottles-%F0%9F%8D%BE-Welcome-to-the-stage-Kylie-%F0%9F%A5%82-Sabrage-j-2-1024x802.jpg)
If you’re after a high-octane night out, bouncing over to Sabrage is well-advised. The acclaimed spectacle melds circus and acrobatic skills with a wardrobe of striking outfits and burlesque performance. Grab a cocktail and some southern bar bites and sit back to enjoy the show – it’s only in town for a limited time!
![The Bayeux Tapestry on display at a museum](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20153925/Bayeux-Tapestry-%C2%A9-Bayeux-Museum-2-min-1024x682.jpg)
The Bayeux Tapestry will return to the UK for the first time in almost 1000 years this September. It’s part of what is expected to be the British Museum’s most popular exhibition ever.
The Bayeux Tapestry is an elaborately embroidered cloth, telling the tale of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings. Spanning a whopping 70 metres, it will find a temporary home at the British Museum, courtesy of a loan agreement made with the Bayeux Museum in Normandy.
![Jack White at his art studio ahead of debut exhibition in London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/17174727/Jack-White-art-studio-1024x683.jpg)
The arrival of the Bayeux Tapestry isn’t the only exciting exhibition coming to London this September. Here are our picks of the best exhibitions to see in London:
💜 Amar Kanwar (September 23, 2026 – January 31, 2027): Serpentine North Gallery – a site-specific installation showcasing Kanwar’s blend of filmmaking, largely exploring the legacies of decolonialisation and the partition of India and Pakistan.
❤️ Marilyn Monroe: A Portrait (Ends September 6): National Portrait Gallery – portraits of the Hollywood icon created by some of the most renowned photographers and artists in the world.
🖤 Modern Toss: “Having an exhibition yeah?” (Ends September 6): The Drawing Room – two decades of work by cartoonists Modern Toss, with 100 pieces, including token-operated swearing machines, big stone heads, large-scale paintings, and more.
🤍 Jack White: THESE THOUGHTS MAY DISAPPEAR (Ends September 13): Newport Street Gallery – Jack White of White Stripes, and, well, Jack White fame, launched his debut visual art exhibition at Damien Hirst’s Newport gallery.
💚 Waldmüller: Landscapes (Ends September 20): The National Gallery – “Discover the breathtaking landscapes of one of Austria’s greatest painters, Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller”
 Trans is Human (Ends September 27): Queer Britain – portraits by renowned photographer Mariano Vivanco that celebrate “thirteen inspiring, familiar and very ordinary transgender people from across the UK.”
 James McNeill Whistler (Ends September 27): Tate Britain – see the infamous ‘Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1’, also known as ‘Whistler’s Mother’ at Europe’s largest retrospective of James McNeill Whistler in 3 decades.
![Various boats moored at a central London marina](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/06101459/PTAIT_20230909_7353-HR-1024x684.jpg)
The Classic Boat Festival returns to St Katharine Docks this September – and it’s completely free to visit! A fleet of beautifully preserved vintage vessels will splash down at central London’s only marina for two days’ worth of maritime merriment. This year, the boats to see and explore include the likes of Dunkirk Little Ships, historic steam tugs, and Thames Sailing Barges.
![a performer leading a parade, twirling brightly coloured cloth around, with an enormous tiger puppet visible in the air behind her](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/03172545/Brick-Lane-Curry-Festival-procession-15_1-1024x683.jpg)
A one-day-only curry festival will fill Brick Lane with flavour, live performances, a parade, giant puppets, and more this September. It’s free to attend, and it’s promising to be “bigger, better and spicier” than before.
Marvel at the Big London Tattoo Show
![a fire performer dancing at the london tattoo show](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/29122113/DSC_2720-1024x731.jpg)
The Big London Tattoo Show returns for its 5th iteration this September – and it’s bigger than ever before. As the UK’s biggest and best tattoo festival, attendees can expect a wealth of artists, demonstrations, live performances and more. The show will feature over 500 artists, live graffiti demonstrations, BMX stunt shows, free fairground rides, and more.
Find out more here.
![Patrick Carney of The Black Keys performs onstage at the 2024 iHeartRadio ALTer EGO Presented by Capital One at the Honda Center on January 13, 2024 in Anaheim, California.](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/05145539/GettyImages-1931289073-1024x683.jpg)
London’s reputation as one of the greatest live music cities in the world is well-earned. From tiny venues showcasing up-and-coming stars to enormous stadium shows, there are countless gigs taking place on any given night in the capital. Here are a few to check out this September:
- The Black Keys (September 1): Brixton Academy
- Geese (September 1-3): Troxy
- The Neighbourhood (September 4): Wembley Arena
- Arijit Singh (September 5): Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
- Hilary Duff (September 10, 15): The O2
- Evanescence (September 13): The O2
- St. Etienne (September 18): The Roundhouse
- Judas Priest (September 21): Hammersmith Apollo
- Death Cab For Cutie (September 25-26): Troxy
- First Aid Kit (September 29): Royal Albert Hall
See a dazzling spectacle on the West End
![text-based poster for RENT the musical with bright neon text](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/18162507/RENT-poster-1024x570.jpg)
London is a world-class theatre destination thanks to its iconic West End. Broadway, who? Find out why this city is so famous for its theatrical productions at these shows this September:
NEW OPENINGS
💖 My Son’s A Queer (But What Can You Do?) (September 16 – October 3): Apollo Theatre – “autobiographical story of West End Musical Theatre star and social-media sensation Rob Madge, as they set out to recreate [a homemade childhood Disney] parade.”
🤣 Hay Fever (September 22 – December 12): Wyndham’s Theatre – Christine Baranski makes her West End debut alongside Richard E. Grant in this eternally relatable Noël Coward comedy.
🧚 Into the Woods (Opens September 22): Noël Coward Theatre – classic fairytales collide as this Sondheim and Lapine classic transfers to the West End.
🎸 Rent (September 26, 2026 – March 27, 2027): Duke of Yorks Theatre – the iconic rock-opera-musical from Jonathan Larson returns to the West End, starring Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo.
ENDING SOON
📜 Cyrano de Bergerac (Ends September 5): Noël Coward Theatre – the Royal Shakespeare Company production transfers to the West End following a sold-out run.
💉 Trainspotting the Musical (Ends September 5): Theatre Royal Haymarket – the cult book-turned-film gets the stage musical treatment.
🪄 Now You See Me Live (Ends September 6): London Coliseum – “World-class illusionists unite for a limited London spectacle” inspired by the film of the same name.
🤫 THE TRUTH a comedy by Florian Zeller (Ends September 12): Apollo Theatre – award-winning and -nominated comedy legends helm this play where two couples navigate a web of hidden truths.
🧠 Arcadia (Ends September 12): Duke of York’s Theatre – the same country house sees two similar stories of genius unfolding, separated by two centuries.
📚 Death Note: The Musical (Ends September 12): Barbican – the acclaimed manga gets a hotly-anticipated musical adaptation for just 50 shows.
🥃 Abigail’s Party (Ends September 19): Harold Pinter Theatre – “Tamzin Outhwaite stars as one of the most iconic characters in British theatre – the unforgettable Beverly in Mike Leigh’s ferocious black comedy of suburban life in the 1970s.”
💔 How The Other Half Loves (Ends September 19): The Old Vic – “Three marriages, two homes, and one terrible alibi meet … [this] comedy on sex, class, and domestic partnerships gone wild.”
🎭 The Oresteia (Ends September 19): Bridge Theatre – “A contemporary family wakes up in a Greek myth and can’t seem to find a way out of their hellish destiny.”
🎤 I’m Every Woman – The Chaka Khan Musical (Ends September 27): Troubadour Wembley Park Theatre – Alexander Burke takes on the role of Chaka Khan.
Or explore the city’s boundary-pushing theatre
![actor Josh O’Connor standing on tarmac in a dark, empty scene, bathed in golden light with his eyes closed](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/18171552/GoldenBoy_Artwork_Website-1024x410.jpg)
The West End isn’t all that London’s theatre scene has to offer! Instead, at London’s off-West End shows, you’ll find some ground-breaking, boundary-pushing theatrical art being made. Check out these productions to see the future faces of the theatre world:
🚘 Thelma & Louise: A New Musical (September 3 – October 24): Young Vic (Main House) – the iconic film gets a new musical treatment.
💭 Darkling (September 5 – October 24): Bush Theatre – a young girl in Bhopal, India, in 1984, dreams of more from life as a giant factory rises over her town.
😨 Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It (September 7 – 26): Soho Theatre – “Two teenagers perform fake Bigfoot sightings in their Appalachian town until a neighbour’s dog turns up torn to pieces.”
🥊 Golden Boy (September 8 – October 31): Almeida Theatre – Emmy and Golden Globe winner Josh O’Connor stars in this revival of Clifford Odets’ “knockout American classic.”
👻 The Turn of the Screw (September 11 – October 10): Arcola Theatre: world premiereof a production based on “the seminal ghost story by Henry James”
🍷 Table 17 (September 17 – October 24): Kiln Theatre – two exes attempt to hash things out after 7 years of not speaking, to find out whether they should give love a second chance.
✍️ Tru (September 19 – November 14): Menier Chocolate Factory – Jesse Tyler Ferguson stars as acclaimed author Truman Capote, alone in his New York apartment after the publication of an excerpt from his tell-all novel Answered Prayers.
Get the pints in for Oktoberfest
![A group of men raising steins of beer at the German Gymnasium in King's Cross, each kitted out in lederhosen and stood behind a table of German delicacies](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/05142340/EV-GermanGym-15Aug23-0788-DB-2-1024x733.jpg)
Despite the name, Oktoberfest traditionally starts in September, not October. Instead, the weeks-long celebration ends in October. Regardless, it’s a spirited celebration of great beer, great food, and great (depending on who you ask) brass bands. Plenty of London venues are honouring the traditional dates with celebrations through September. Head here for pints a-plenty:
🍺 DAS HARVEST FEST at Villages Brewery (September 11 & 12) – while not technically an Oktoberfest event, this celebration of the harvest (and lager) from Hop Burns & Black and Villages is in the same spirit as the other celebrations.
🍻 Albert’s Schloss (September 19 – October 25) – over a month of sudsy Bavaraian celebration and feasting awaits you at this enormous bier palace in the middle of London.
🍺 German Gymnasium (September 18 – October 23) – “Bavarian Spezialitäten, German beers, live Oompah performances and a season of celebrations in the heart of King’s Cross.”
🍻 Bermondsey Bierkellar (September 19 – October 31) – “Bigger. Louder. Unforgettable. London’s wildest Oktoberfest returns.”
summary: London offers a wide variety of events, festivals, and exhibitions throughout September. Highlights include music events like Waterworks Extended and the London Open House Festival, alongside cultural celebrations such as Black on the Square and celebrASIA. Additionally, major exhibitions like the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum and the Classic Boat Festival provide diverse entertainment options for visitors.
key_points: The Bayeux Tapestry returns to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years for an exhibition at the British Museum.
The London Open House Festival allows public access to exclusive buildings and historical sites across the city.
Free cultural events like celebrASIA, Black on the Square, and the Classic Boat Festival take place during September.

title: Windrush line disrupted after fire at South Bermondsey waste centre
author: Harry Low; James W Kelly; Yang Tian
content:
Video shows moments after the fire broke out
- Published
Some London Overground trains remain suspended after a fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste "severely damaged" a recycling facility in south-east London.
Fifteen fire engines were called to Landmann Way in South Bermondsey shortly before 20:00 BST on Tuesday, according to London Fire Brigade (LFB), which said the fire was brought under control six hours later.
No services are running on the Windrush line from Surrey Quays to New Cross and Clapham Junction "due to an unsafe structure next to the railway". Trains from Highbury and Islington to West Croydon are severely delayed.
The LFB said the cause of the fire was not yet known. Firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June.
Speaking from the scene, station commander Duncan Rees said: "Crews worked hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control."
He added that ladders were used to tackle the flames from above.
![Smoke rises over buildings. River Thames is in foreground](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d491/live/715ebd70-9b96-11f1-8663-5b9301c10e82.jpg)
London Fire Brigade received more than 160 reports of a fire
Crews from East Greenwich, Old Kent Road, Deptford and surrounding fire stations were dispatched to the scene.
Rail services into London Bridge from New Cross were affected due to the fire blocking railway lines, National Rail said.
"Trains between these stations may be cancelled, severely delayed by up to 100 minutes or revised," it said on Tuesday.
![A cyclist watches besides a blue railing as plumes of black smoke drift into the sky above the yellow recycling facility.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/94a9/live/8b443d10-9b9a-11f1-a4e6-dfdb59e74cb0.jpg)
The fire caused rail disruption between London Bridge and New Cross
Rachael Jardine, a freelance journalist based in New Cross, told BBC London that trains on a nearby overground track were continuing to pass despite the "thick black smoke".
A local resident said he had first spotted the blaze while cycling home.
"I was coming back from Tescos and I could see the smoke from the road," he said.
"We cycled back to mine and realised it was just across the road... it's pretty mental."

summary: A fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste severely damaged a recycling facility in South Bermondsey, requiring 15 fire engines and six hours to bring under control. The incident has caused ongoing disruption and suspensions on the London Overground Windrush line due to an unsafe structure next to the railway. The cause of the fire is currently unknown, though the same facility experienced a blaze previously in June.
key_points: A fire broke out at a recycling facility on Landmann Way in South Bermondsey involving 50 tonnes of household waste.
London Overground services on the Windrush line remain suspended between Surrey Quays, New Cross, and Clapham Junction.
The suspension is due to an unsafe structure next to the railway resulting from the fire.
The London Fire Brigade brought the blaze under control after six hours, and the cause is not yet known.
